progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: Read formulas and an already-balanced equation; calculate formula molar mass; use n=m/M and m=nM; choose a wanted/known coefficient ratio. Empirical formulas is not a compulsory prerequisite.
progression.startsWith: Carbon dioxide can outweigh its starting carbon because oxygen also contributes mass.
progression.stopsAfter: Predict and interpret a theoretical mass in either direction using species molar masses, balanced coefficients and stated assumptions.
progression.nextLesson: Limiting reactants: compare two finite reactant supplies before predicting product and excess.

teaching.task: Predict a theoretical reacting or product mass from a balanced equation, using each species molar mass and stated conditions.
teaching.causalExplanation: Balanced coefficients compare amounts, not grams. Each species molar mass links mass and amount; different compositions explain why equal mole amounts need not have equal mass. Added oxygen and oxygen transferred to CO₂ preserve mass accounting.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Open with a concrete mass surprise, explain why the relationships work, then compare a unit-ratio carbon case with a non-unit oxide case. Working carries repeated arithmetic; narration connects the stages and interprets the result. Numerical guard digits and exact supplied constants stay on stable boards; speech explains approximate amounts and the chemical relationship, then reports the final precision.
teaching.openingDecision: About 44 g CO₂ from 12 g carbon: where did the extra mass come from? Include oxygen in the initial system rather than implying a conservation exception.
